title: How to use tax-efficient investing strategies in a taxable US brokerage account
description: Keeping more of your returns by managing dividends, turnover, and harvesting.
content:
Once you have maxed out your 401(k) and IRA, the next step is the Taxable Brokerage Account. Unlike retirement accounts, the IRS watches every move here. Every dividend you receive and every share you sell generates a tax bill. If you aren't careful, you can lose 1% to 2% of your annual returns to 'Tax Drag.' However, with smart management—specifically 'Asset Location' and 'Tax Loss Harvesting'—you can make a taxable account nearly as efficient as an IRA.

Key Takeaways

  • Asset Location: Put 'Tax-Efficient' assets (ETFs, Stocks) in your brokerage. Put 'Tax-Inefficient' assets (Bonds, REITs) in your IRA. This simple sorting saves massive taxes.
  • ETFs > Mutual Funds: ETFs rarely distribute capital gains due to their unique creation/redemption structure. They are the preferred vehicle for taxable accounts.
  • Tax Loss Harvesting (TLH): The silver lining of a crash. Selling a loser allows you to bank a tax deduction to offset future gains or ordinary income ($3,000/year).
  • Qualified Dividends: Ensure you hold dividend stocks for >60 days to get the lower 15% tax rate instead of your income tax rate.

Why It Matters (US Context)

The US tax code is progressive. Short-term gains are taxed at your highest marginal rate (up to 37%). Long-term gains are taxed at 0%, 15%, or 20%. The goal of taxable investing is to *never* pay short-term capital gains tax.

The 'Do Not Buy' List for Taxable Accounts

Avoid holding these assets in a brokerage account if possible.

1. REITs (Real Estate Investment Trusts)

Why: By law, they pay out 90% of income. These dividends are usually 'Non-Qualified,' meaning they are taxed at your full income tax rate (e.g., 32%). Keep them in an IRA.

2. Corporate Bond Funds

Why: Interest payments are taxed as Ordinary Income. High tax drag. Use Municipal Bonds instead (Tax-Free).

3. High-Turnover Active Funds

Why: If the fund manager buys and sells stocks frequently, they generate short-term capital gains that are passed on to you. You get a tax bill even if the fund lost value.

The Harvesting Protocol

  1. Monitor for Losses: If the market drops 10%, look at your specific lots. Do you have a position down $2,000?
  2. Execute the Swap: Sell the loser (e.g., VTI). Immediately buy a 'Substantially Identical' replacement (e.g., SCHB).
  3. The Result: You are still invested in the US market (so you don't miss the rebound), but you booked a $2,000 loss on your tax return.
  4. The Limit: You can use losses to offset unlimited gains. If you have net losses, you can deduct $3,000 against your salary. Carry forward the rest forever.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Wash Sale Rule?

If you sell a stock for a loss and buy the exact same stock back within 30 days, the IRS disallows the loss. You must buy something different (e.g., switching from S&P 500 to Total Market).

Should I reinvest dividends?

In a taxable account, consider turning DRIP OFF. Take the cash. Use it to rebalance. This prevents creating hundreds of tiny 'tax lots' that are annoying to track.

Is it worth the effort?

Yes. Tax Loss Harvesting can add ~0.50% to your annual after-tax returns. Over 30 years, that is huge.
